summary: Specifies the Russian Dolls bandwidth constraints model for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. In this model, limits are nested so that each traffic class sits inside a larger allowance, like nested dolls. This is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: The Russian Dolls Model defines nested bandwidth limits for traffic classes in Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering. A class's limit also accounts for the classes nested within it.

subtitle: A bandwidth-constraint model for Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering.

tldr.problem: Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering needs a way to enforce different bandwidth limits for different classes of traffic on a link.
tldr.mechanism: The Russian Dolls Model sets nested bandwidth constraints. Each constraint limits the total reserved bandwidth for one class and all higher-numbered classes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4127 is Experimental. It specifies one bandwidth-constraint model and assigns it model identifier 0.

today: RFC 4127 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. It defines the Russian Dolls Model as one bandwidth-constraint model for DS-TE.

sections.title: Classes and Bandwidth Constraints
sections.content:
Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering (DS-TE) can assign different bandwidth constraints to different classes of traffic. RFC 4127 describes one such model, the Russian Dolls Model (RDM), for use with the protocol extensions specified in RFC 4124.

A Class-Type groups traffic trunks that use the same bandwidth constraints on a link. A TE-Class pairs a Class-Type with a preemption priority that an MPLS label switched path may use when it is set up or held.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can place traffic into classes and give each class a bandwidth limit. RDM defines how these limits apply to a class and the classes grouped within it.

sections.title: The Nested Limits
sections.content:
RDM supports at most 8 Class-Types and 8 corresponding Bandwidth Constraints. For each constraint BCb, the sum of reserved bandwidth for Class-Types b and above must not exceed BCb. BC0 is the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth and limits the sum across all classes.

For example, an administrator could set BC0 to 2.5 Gb/s for voice and data together, and BC1 to 1.5 Gb/s for voice. The wider limit applies to all traffic; the narrower limit applies to a subset.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bandwidth constraint limits a group of classes, and a wider constraint includes the classes inside it. BC0 sets the limit for all classes combined.

sections.title: Calculating Available Bandwidth
sections.content:
A router implementing RDM must enforce the defined constraints. When it calculates unreserved bandwidth for a TE-Class, it must account for all bandwidth constraints that apply to that class and its preemption priority.

The RFC gives example formulas but says detailed admission-control algorithms are outside the scope of the IETF work. It also says BC0 equals Maximum Reservable Bandwidth, so a router receiving both values may ignore the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth sub-TLV when using RDM.
sections.plainLanguage: A router checks every nested limit that applies before treating bandwidth as available. The RFC gives example calculations but does not prescribe a complete admission-control algorithm.

sections.title: Preemption and Model Trade-Offs
sections.content:
RDM allows preemption within a Class-Type and across Class-Types. Used with preemption, the model can provide isolation between classes while preserving bandwidth efficiency and protection against quality-of-service degradation.

If an administrator prohibits preemption, RDM can still support bandwidth efficiency and QoS protection, but it cannot guarantee isolation between Class-Types. The RFC says security considerations for DS-TE are addressed by the companion protocol document, RFC 4124.
sections.plainLanguage: Preemption can help RDM keep one class's bandwidth separate from another's. Without preemption, the model cannot guarantee that separation.
